en: Preface by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, Chapter One: The Preface. It is difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world; it is difficult for a Buddha to preach this [Dharma]; it is difficult to transmit and translate this difficulty; it is difficult to attain self-awakening; it is difficult to hear a teacher’s exposition; and it is difficult to memorize it after hearing it but once.

I, Yu, listened to and received these teachings at Jinling when I was twenty-seven, and I revised and edited them at Danqiu when I was sixty-nine. I leave them as a gift to future worthies, hoping that we may together aspire to the Buddha-wisdom.
The detailed explanation of the title of the sutra has already been stated above.

As for the term "Preface" (*xu*), it is glossed as "orderly sequence" (*xiangxu*); this means that the stages, the roles of host and guest, and the questions and answers are all conducted with orderly propriety.
The sūtra compiler follows the meaning [of these terms], taking them to mean "sequence," "source," and "narration.
These five matters are placed at the beginning of the sūtra: "sequence" refers to the arrangement;
"source" refers to the six auspicious omens of the emission of light that serve as the catalyst for the teaching's inception.
The "Preface" (序) consists of questions and answers to resolve doubts, the formal exposition as an introduction, and the narrative account.
Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called a "Preface.
As for "Chapter" (品), the *Madhyama Āgama* refers to it as *varga*, which is translated here as "Chapter" (品).
Regarding "fascicles" (*pin*): when items of similar meaning and category are gathered into a single section, it is called a fascicle.
Sometimes the Buddha himself proclaims the fascicles, as in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*;
sometimes they are established by the compilers of the canon, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Alternatively, it may be that the translators added [these passages], as was the case with Kumārajīva.
Now, the "Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga*) is what the Buddha himself proclaimed;
however, the "Wonderful Sound" (*Gandavyūha*), the "Avalokiteśvara," and others were not heard by the compilers of the sūtras or the translators.
Because it is the beginning of all chapters, it is called "the first.

Regarding the Buddha’s two teachings on the scattering of flowers and the stringing of flowers in response to conditions, the compilers transmitted them according to what was taught, and the commentators expounded upon them based on the sūtras; in neither case were they categorized into specific sections.

Ancient lecturers merely expounded the broad principles of the meaning without dividing them into chapters and sections; if one were to employ this approach exclusively, later generations would likely fail to recognize the beginning and end [of the discourse].
Furthermore, the Buddha’s teachings consist of both integrated and scattered [passages], and the compilers established chapters according to their respective meanings.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states:
"A portion of the Sūtras, a portion of the Vinaya, and a portion of the Abhidharma.
Furthermore, the Sūtras are divided into four categories: namely, the *Ekottarika*, the *Dīrgha*, the *Madhyama*, and the *Saṃyukta*.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* clarifies the causes and effects for humans and devas; the *Dīrgha Āgama* refutes false views; the *Madhyama Āgama* elucidates profound meanings; and the *Saṃyukta Āgama* elucidates meditative concentration.
The Vinaya opens with the five divisions and the eighty recitations;
the Abhidharma opens with the *Ṣaṭpāda* and the *Aṣṭagrantha*, etc.;
and the Āgamas refer to:
“Generosity, precepts, wisdom, and the six perfections are all complete; this refers to the eightfold collection consisting of faculties, nature, path, concentration, and so forth.

In his treatise, Vasubandhu assigns the *Introduction Chapter* (*Nidāna-parivarta*) to seven categories of merit, the *Chapter on Expedient Means* (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*) to five manifestations, and the remaining chapters are each allocated accordingly.
In the past, Peng of Hexi and Yao of Jiangdong took this principle as the framework for their commentaries; in later generations, they became increasingly prolix.

As the Guangzhai era progressed, the details became even more minute, casting a heavy mist that obscured the Great Clarity (Taiqing), causing the Three Luminaries to withdraw their radiance—a state not esteemed by those seeking the Way.
Tanyuan said: "Fine incense smoke drifts upward, and mixed abrasive dust flies about.
This refers, respectively, to going too far and falling short.
The Dragon Master of Mount Lu divided the text into the Prologue, the Main Body, and the Circulation. The twenty-seven chapters are subsumed under only two categories:
from the "Prologue" to the "Dharma Master," which speak of the provisional and the ultimate, for while the principle is one, the teaching is threefold;
from the "Jeweled Stupa" onwards, which concern the provisional and ultimate aspects of the body, for the reality is remote while the manifestation is near.
Furthermore, from the "Expedient Means" chapter to the "Peaceful Practices" chapter constitutes the gate of causes, while from the "Emergence" chapter downward constitutes the gate of fruits.
This division of the text is identical to that of Zhongxing Yin and Xiaoshan Yao, who received the sutra from [Master] Long.

Xuanchang [divides the sutra] such that from the "Preface" to the "Many Treasures Stupa" constitutes the causal section; from the "Exhortation to Uphold" to the "Supernatural Powers" constitutes the resultant section; and from the "Entrustment" to the end of the scripture constitutes the section on protection and preservation.
Furthermore, another master says:
"From the 'Introduction' to the 'Record of Those Who Are Learners and Those Beyond Learning' constitutes the essence of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
from the 'Dharma Master' to the 'Entrustment' clarifies the merit of receiving and upholding [the teaching]."
From the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter to the end of the sutra, it extols the original vows of the various bodhisattvas.
Some masters divide this into four sections:
the first chapter constitutes the introductory section;
From the "Expedient Means" chapter to the "Peaceful Conduct," the three [vehicles] are opened to reveal the One Vehicle;
from the "Emergence" chapter through the "Discrimination of Merits," the near is opened to reveal the distant;
and what follows thereafter is the section on the continued circulation [of the teaching].

Guangzhai received the sutra from Yuncong; its first three sections each open into two parts: namely, the general introduction (tongxu) and the specific introduction (biexu); the main body (zheng) consists of the gate of causes (yinmen) and the gate of results (guomen); and the circulation (liutong) refers to the transformation of others and one's own practice.
The two prefaces each have five sections, the two main bodies each have four, and the two concluding sections each have three; thus, there are twenty-four segments in total.

Now, the division of the scriptural text is entirely a matter of human convention; as the orchid and the chrysanthemum each excel in their own beauty, those of later generations should not engage in disputes of right and wrong, for such actions yield no benefit and cause one to lose the singular Way.
The "three benefits" refer to the three *siddhāntas*, such as the worldly;
the "one path" refers to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
Tiantai Zhiyi divided the text into these three sections.
The first chapter serves as the introduction;
from the "Expedient Means" chapter up to the nineteenth line of the "Discrimination of Merits" chapter—comprising fifteen and a half chapters—is termed the "Correct" [Teaching].
From the verse following that point to the end of the sutra—comprising eleven and a half chapters—is termed the "Circulation."
Furthermore, the text is divided into two parts:
from the Introduction through the fourteen chapters ending with "Peaceful Conduct" (*Anle-xing*), the provisional is opened and the real is revealed in terms of the traces (*ji*);
from the "Emergence" (*Yongchu*) chapter until the end of the scripture—comprising fourteen chapters—the provisional is opened and the real is revealed in terms of the fundamental (*ben*).
The text consists of the Prologue, the Main Body, and the Dissemination, each with its own sequence.

The first chapter constitutes the Prologue; from the "Expedient Means" chapter through the "Bestowal of Predictions upon Learners and Those Beyond Learning" chapter constitutes the Main Body; and from the "Dharma Master" chapter through the "Peaceful Practices" chapter constitutes the Dissemination.
The section from the conclusion of the "Emergence" (踊出) up to "Maitreya has already asked this matter, and the Buddha now answers it"—half a chapter—is called the Introduction (序).
From "The Buddha addressed Ajita" downwards, up to the verses at the end of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" (分別功德品), is called the Main Body (正).
Everything following this until the end of the sutra constitutes the Dissemination (流通).
Now, I shall provide a commentary on the text based on the preceding three sections.
Question:
How can a single sūtra have two prefaces?

Answer: The *Avataṃsaka* assembles the multitude in various places, and every chapter of the *Āgama* is likewise so; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* entrusts [the teaching] at both its beginning and end. Since none of these contradict their respective sections, how could there be any obstruction between the two orders?
The reason the five meanings are not established here is that the Original Gate (Honmon) is not the primary sequence.

As for the Trace Gate (Jikimon) being merely for the sake of circulation, it is because the preaching of the Dharma has not yet reached its conclusion; such is the meaning of "existence" and "non-existence."
The present postscript consists of four parts:
first, the enumeration; second, the reason why;
[third, the citation; fourth, the conclusion].
Third, citing scriptural evidence;
fourth, indicating the characteristics.
Regarding the enumeration:
There are four methods of interpretation: first, by causes and conditions; second, by the teachings; third, by the original and the manifested; and fourth, by contemplating the mind.

From the beginning with "Thus have I heard" to the end with "and withdrew," all passages are analyzed through these four intentions. Here, I have written them briefly—sometimes using three, two, or even one method—valuing the attainment of the intended meaning rather than the proliferation of words.
2. Regarding the reason for this: Question:
If summarized, there is only one; if expanded, there are not merely four. Why is this so? Answer:

If explained extensively, it would cause the intellect to retreat; if explained too briefly, the meaning would not be comprehensive. I now speak by taking the middle way, so that the meaning may be easily understood.

"Causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) is also termed "stimulus and response" (ganying). Although sentient beings do not perceive [the Buddha] when they are near due to a lack of spiritual capacity (indriya), the power of the roots of goodness in his compassion naturally reaches them from afar. Because the paths of stimulus and response intersect, I employ the explanation of causes and conditions.
Now, as sentient beings seek liberation, these capacities are manifold;
as the Sages arise to respond, these responses are likewise manifold.
This principle becomes even more extensive—wherein does the "Middle" reside?
However, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"The power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness has immeasurable gateways; briefly stated, these are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). When the spiritual resonance of sentient beings in the ten directions occurs, it is as vast as empty space."

Now, regarding the Buddha’s work through sound within the Sahā world, the gate of ambrosia has opened; this shall be clarified according to the teachings in the *Zhongshenming* (Exposition on the Names of the Central Deity).

If one establishes the teaching in response to the capacities of sentient beings, the teachings differ in terms of provisional and ultimate, as well as shallow and deep; one must set aside the finger to preserve the moon, and abandon the traces to seek the source.
Therefore, Master Zhao said:
"Without the fundamental (ben), there would be no way to manifest the traces (ji); without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental.
Thus, I employ the explanation of the fundamental and the traces.

If one seeks the traces, the traces are vast and lead only to wearying oneself; if one seeks the source, the source is high and lofty, beyond reach. Day and night one counts the treasures of others, yet for oneself there is not even half a coin’s worth. One should simply contemplate the height and breadth of one's own mind and strike the infinite resonance of the Sage; when the capacity is perfected, it brings forth a response, leading to the attainment of one’s own benefit. Therefore, I employ the contemplation of the mind as the explanation.
Third, the citation of scriptural evidence.
The "Expedient Means" chapter states:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions appear in the world for the sake of the single great causal condition."

If beings of the human or celestial realms, or those of the Lesser Vehicle, were not "one," nor "great," and furthermore, if it were not a Buddha-activity, the responsive resonance with sentient beings would not be established.
True reality is called "one," and its vastness is called "great"; the Buddha takes this as his "activity" and appears in the world—this is termed the "One Great Matter of Cause and Condition."
It is further said:
"By means of various Dharma-gates, one proclaims and reveals the Buddha-way.

One should know that these various vocal teachings—whether subtle or manifest, whether provisional or ultimate—all serve as fishing weirs for the sake of the Buddha-way. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
This refers to the statement: "Both harsh words and gentle speech ultimately converge upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
As it says in the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*):
"Today, gods, humans, and asuras all say that I left home while still young, departed from the palace of the Śākyas, and attained perfect enlightenment not far from the city of Gayā."

"However, in truth, since I first attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; by means of these skillful means (*upāya*), I have guided and benefited sentient beings.
The "Expedient Means" chapter further states:
"I originally established this vow: to cause all beings everywhere to likewise attain this Way, so that they are no different from us."
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred" states:

"Internally they conceal their bodhisattva practices, while externally they manifest as śrāvakas; in reality they purify their own buddha-fields, yet they show themselves to the multitude as possessing the three poisons and even manifesting the signs of false views.
My disciples act in this way, using skillful means to deliver sentient beings."
"In this way, both master and disciple clarify their fundamental and manifested traces," and so forth.
The "Parable Chapter" states:
"If anyone believes what you have said, they shall see me, and they shall also see you, as well as the assembly of bhikṣus and all the bodhisattvas."
"You should know that according to whatever you have heard, you must examine it with a mind of truth; within a mind of faith, you will behold the Three Jewels:
hearing this teaching is seeing the Jewel of the Dharma; seeing me is seeing the Jewel of the Buddha; and seeing you all is seeing the Jewel of the Saṃgha," and so forth.
Fourth, regarding the demonstration of signs: for the time being, we shall illustrate the signs of causes and conditions by way of three stages.

For a long time, sentient beings have been favored by the Buddha’s skillful means, which has caused them to plant the causes and conditions for the Buddha-way; subsequently, upon meeting him in the interim, he further employs diverse expedient means to assist in revealing the primary meaning and brings them to maturity.
Today, flowers rain down and the earth trembles; they bring about nirvana through the nirvana of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, those who have long planted the seeds, matured them in the past, and attained liberation in the present age—such as those who emerged from the earth—are examples of this.

Furthermore, the intermediate state is the seed, the four tastes are the ripening, and the royal city is liberation; these refer to those who are currently undergoing the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
Furthermore, the present life is the seed, the next life is the ripening, and future lives are liberation; these refer to those who will attain deliverance in the future.
Although this is not yet the main teaching, it is spoken by taking its essential meaning.
Within these sections, treating each stage as the three periods or nine periods—of planting, ripening, and liberation—is likewise without hindrance.
For what reason?
It is because the Tathāgata teaches with mastery through the power of his sovereign supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and with the powerful, fierce, and majestic force of a lion’s springing leap.
Because of such qualities as these, there is the introductory section (*nidāna*).

The assembly beheld these rare and auspicious omens and, with reverent longing, desired to hear the complete Way. The Buddha, responding to their capacity, established his transformation through teaching, opening, revealing, awakening, and entering them into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thus there is the Section on the Correct Exposition.

Not only did they obtain great benefit at that time, but even during the distant period of the final five hundred years, they were deeply moistened by the wondrous Way; therefore, there is the "Circulation" section.

Furthermore, regarding the indication of the characteristics of the teaching: this introduction is not written as an introduction for the pure ascent of humans and devas, nor as an introduction for the minor paths of the two vehicles, nor as an introduction for those who realize emptiness and pass through the three vehicles, nor as an introduction for the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas alone; rather, it is an introduction for the direct relinquishing of expedient means and the preaching solely of the unsurpassed Buddha-way.

This "correct" does not refer to the mundane as correct; it does not refer to the analytical wisdom of firefly-light as correct; it does not refer to the wisdom of the essence of dharmas, like a lamp or torch, as correct; nor does it refer to the path-variety wisdom of stars and moon as correct; rather, it refers to the all-encompassing wisdom of the sun's light as correct.

This circulation is not for the purpose of circulating the "leaves of willow" or the "wooden ox and wooden horse"; it is not a circulation of the half-syllables, nor a circulation of the common syllables, nor a circulation of the distinct syllables; it is purely a circulation of the perfect *sūtra* of the full-syllable Dharma.

Next, regarding the demonstration of the original and the trace: when [the Buddha] practiced the bodhisattva path for a long, distant time, he proclaimed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* of previous Buddhas; this also possesses the three divisions of superior, middling, and inferior discourse, and likewise possesses the original and the trace. However, if one were to compare Buddha after Buddha, these would be infinite. Therefore, we specifically take the superior, middling, and inferior discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* spoken at the time of his initial attainment of Buddhahood, designating it specifically as "superior" and naming it the "original."
Why is this? Because he first attained Buddhahood and first preached the Dharma, he is the supreme and the fundamental; this meaning should be understood.

His intermediate activities of transformation—assisting Buddhas such as Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and Dīpaṃkara to proclaim the three sections of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—are merely termed "intermediate" and merely termed "traces."
Why is this? Because there was that which preceded it as superior, and there was that which preceded it as fundamental.

The three divisions taught today in the royal city are merely designated as inferior and merely designated as traces; even the power of the lion’s vigorous springing is likewise so. As for the three divisions to be taught eternally in the future, they too shall point to the very beginning as being superior and fundamental.

For example, although a great tree may have thousands of branches and ten thousand leaves, when one discusses its root, it cannot be said that each branch points back to another to indicate a common origin; this analogy can be understood in this way, and so forth.

Next, to demonstrate the contemplation of the mind's characteristics: one should discuss precept, concentration, and wisdom in relation to one’s own mind as three divisions—cultivating them with precepts first, concentration in the middle, and wisdom last.
If considered as a dharma-gate, however, wisdom is the root, while concentration and precepts are the traces.

Furthermore, morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) each consist of three parts: the preliminary practices and the conclusion of the formal ritual of the fourfold motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) constitute the three parts of morality;

the twenty-five expedient means, correct contemplation throughout all conditions, and skillfully entering, abiding in, and emerging from hundreds of thousands of samādhis constitute the three parts of concentration;
and the principle that "all phenomena produced through causes and conditions are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle" constitutes the three parts of wisdom.
Having already demonstrated the four kinds of characteristics by means of the three divisions, one should apply this principle.
From the words "Thus" (*evam*) up until "having paid homage, they withdrew," the entire text should be interpreted through these four intentions.

It is easy to understand this meaning by relying on analogy and comparison, but difficult to analyze and demonstrate it through words; let the practitioner contemplate this well: though the expressions differ, the intent is the same—a thousand chariots share one track, and ten thousand streams meet at the salty sea.
The introduction consists of both the general and the specific. From "Thus" up to "sat down to one side" is the general introduction;
from "At that time, the World-Honored One" up to the end of the chapter is the specific introduction.
The general introduction (sūtra-pūrva-nidāna) applies to all teachings;
the specific introduction (pratyeka-pūrva-nidāna) pertains to a single sūtra.
The general introduction consists of five, six, or seven [sections], and so forth.
"Thus" (evam) refers to the essence of the Dharma as it was heard.
"I heard" (śrutam mayā) refers to the person who was able to retain it.
"At one time" (ekasmin samaye) signifies the harmony between hearing and retaining; it does not mean that they occurred at different times.
"Buddha" refers to hearing [the teaching] from the Buddha at that time.
"The Royal City and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa" refers to the place where it was heard and upheld.
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus" refers to the companions who heard and upheld it.
All these arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, produced in successive succession.

Furthermore, as for "Thus" (evam): at the beginning of the sutras of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, the word "Thus" is invariably placed; this signifies that the Way of all Buddhas is identical and does not contend with the world—this is the *loka-samvṛti* (worldly standpoint).
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"To cause people to give rise to faith at the very moment [the teaching] is presented" refers to the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint established for the benefit of individuals).
Furthermore, "to refute the heterodox views that 'A' and 'O' are inferior or incorrect" refers to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedy).

Moreover, the term "thus" (*evam*) is a word of faithful compliance: through faith, the principles one has heard are integrated; through compliance, the path between teacher and disciple is perfected—this is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth).
The explanation based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is extremely extensive and cannot be recorded in full, and so forth.

As for the explanation according to the teachings (*yàojiào shì*), the Sūtra states that the Buddhadharma of the three periods of time all begins in this same way. Previous Buddhas had sūtras categorized as gradual, sudden, secret, and indeterminate; the gradual further included the *Tripiṭaka*, the Shared (*tōng*), the Distinct (*bié*), and the Perfect (*yuán*).
The present Buddha is likewise so; since the various sūtras differ, their methods of exposition are also diverse, and one should not attempt to open many doors with a single key.
Furthermore, the two texts—those of the Buddha and Ānanda—are not different in their nature as "suchness" (tathatā), and that which expresses is capable of expressing that which is expressed.
Now, what text did Ānanda transmit from the Buddha, and what is it that he expresses?

One cannot transmit the sudden through gradual texts, nor can one expound the perfect through partial texts; if the transmission and exposition are erroneous, then the texts are inadequate, and if the texts are inadequate, then the principle is not correctly realized.
This meaning is difficult to clarify and requires careful and detailed examination.
For now, following the gradual teaching, the Buddha clarifies that conventional reality possesses words and letters, whereas ultimate reality is devoid of words and letters.

Ānanda transmitted the Buddha’s words regarding conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) in written form; as these do not differ from what the Buddha spoke, they are called "Thus" (evam). Because one attains the principle of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) through these conventional texts, they are called "So" (iti). This is how the opening of the Tripiṭaka sūtras clarifies the phrase "Thus it has been."

The Buddha’s clarity is that form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form; form and emptiness, emptiness and form, are without duality and without distinction. That emptiness and form are not different is "thusness" (tathatā); that reality is found within phenomena is "suchness" (bhūtatā).

That Ānanda’s transmission of the Buddha’s words is no different [from the truth] constitutes "Thus" (evam); that the expressive means are identical to the expressed meaning constitutes "This" (iti). This is the "Thus and This" at the beginning of the sutras of the Shared Teaching (p’ung-chiao).

The Buddha clarifies that birth-and-death has a limit and nirvāṇa is limitless; one emerges from the limit of birth-and-death and enters the limitlessness of nirvāṇa; emerging from the limitlessness of nirvāṇa, one enters the Middle Way.

Ānanda transmitted this teaching of emerging from existence into non-existence, and emerging from non-existence into the Middle Way; it is identical to what the Buddha taught and is thus "Thus" (evam). From the shallow to the profound, there is nothing that is not "is. This constitutes the beginning of the "Thus" in the Separate Teaching (pratyeka-yāna) sūtras.
The Buddha clarifies that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa* and is also the Middle Way; how much more so, then, could *nirvāṇa* not be the Middle Way?

Suchness (*tathatā*), the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the true nature (*bhūtatathatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) pervade all places, such that there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma.

Ānanda transmitted this in a manner no different from what the Buddha had spoken; therefore, it is called "Thus" (tathā). Because it is suchness (tathatā) and immovable, it is called "So" (iti). This constitutes the opening phrase "Thus have I heard" of the Perfect Sūtra.
If one moves from the conventional to enter the suchness, this is the meaning of the Tripiṭaka;
if one does not move from the conventional and it is itself suchness, this is the meaning of the Shared Teaching;
if one moves within suchness to enter suchness, this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching.
"The immovable suchness is itself suchness; this is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching," and so forth.

If sudden suchness were identical to the Perfect, or if indefinite suchness involved mutual alternation between prior and subsequent stages, these would be "secret" matters, hidden and not transmitted.
One spreads the net of the eight teachings across the ocean of the Dharma-realm; fearing that beings may have outflows, how could one single eye of the net be stretched out in isolation?
Furthermore, to receive four arrows at once without letting them fall to the ground cannot yet be called a feat of swiftness;
if one cannot even manage one arrow when urging on a dull donkey or driving a lame tortoise, how much less so for four? And so forth.

To explain this according to the provisional and the real (honji-suijaku): throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, both horizontally and vertically, it is exactly thus. The past is far-reaching, the present is vast, and the future is eternal—all are entirely like this; where, then, is the origin?
What constitutes a "trace"?
Taking the initial attainment of the Way by Śākyamuni Buddha as our standard, those instances where the beginning of a sutra is as it is described therein constitute the "origin.
Those instances where the beginning of a sutra spoken today—following his intermediate activities as a Buddha—is likewise described are all "traces."
Furthermore, that which was transmitted by Ānanda is the "trace" (the manifestation), while that which was spoken by the Buddha is the "root" (the essence).
Moreover, that the Master and disciple have both attained such realization is not something that began only today, nor did it begin in the interim;
this is the root. That which occurred in the interim and today is the trace.

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: contemplating that all such meanings as the traces of the *siddhānta* teachings and so forth are entirely phenomena produced by causes and conditions constitutes the general contemplation (*sāmānyālambana*).
That causes and conditions are themselves emptiness and provisionality constitutes the specific contemplation (*viśeṣālambana*).

Taking these two contemplations as the path of skillful means to enter the Middle Way of the ultimate truth and simultaneously illumine the two truths constitutes both the general and the specific contemplation.
The statement that "all the above is the Middle Way" refers to neither the general nor the specific contemplation.
As the text below states:
"If a person believes what you have said, they will immediately see me, as well as you, the assembly of bhikṣus, and all the bodhisattvas."
This is precisely the clear exposition of contemplative practice (*guanxing*).
Faith refers to the capacity of the recipient, while vision refers to the response of the teacher; this is the principle of causes and conditions (*nidāna*).

Furthermore, there are varying degrees of depth in faith and distinctions between provisional and ultimate in vision; these various differentiations constitute the categorized teachings (*fenbie jiao*).

Furthermore, by believing in the text of the *Lotus Sūtra*, one perceives the essence of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); if one perceives the transformation of Śāriputra, one perceives the essence of Nāgārjuna;
if one perceives the initial attainment of Buddhahood by Śākyamuni, one also perceives the ancient Buddhas who attained it long ago;
and if one perceives the twelve hundred bhikṣus and eighty thousand bodhisattvas, one likewise perceives their fundamental essence.
Furthermore, when one hears the sutras and believes them with a mind free from doubt, perceiving this faith as luminous and pure is seeing the Buddha;
when the factors of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) are clearly discerned, it is seeing Śāriputra;
when all the various factors are clearly discerned, it is seeing the assembly of bhikṣus.
With a mind purified by compassion, one beholds all the bodhisattvas.

Regarding the mind, there are four sections of commentary that become increasingly clear; however, when commenting on other sutras, only three points are employed, because they serve to reveal the traces [of the Buddha] for those who have not yet awakened their fundamental nature.
It should be understood that three of the present commentaries on this sūtra are identical to others, while one commentary differs from them; thus concludes the fourfold explanation, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), or alternatively "Thus [it was] heard," these variations likely arise because different manuscript versions of the sūtra were circulated, with each version citing either the beginning or the end of the formula.
Now, I shall provide four explanations by way of illustration. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"When the faculty of hearing is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and one directs the mind with the desire to hear—through the convergence of these various conditions—one says, 'I have heard.'"
Question: One should say "heard by the ear"; why then do you say "heard by me"? Answer:
"I am the master of the ear; I raise it up and encompass all conditions.
This is the explanation of the World-Honored One.

Ānanda ascended the high seat and proclaimed, "I have heard," while the great assembly responded with mournful wailing. Just as they beheld the Tathāgata, he now proclaimed, "I have heard," and those beyond training (aśaikṣas) soared through the air and recited verses.

The *Buddhaghoṣa-sūtra* clearly states that when Mañjuśrī presided over the compilation, he first proclaimed the title and then recited "Thus have I heard," at which point the assembly wailed in grief.
This is the explanation for human beings.

Ānanda ascended the high seat and proclaimed "Thus have I heard," thereby dispelling the doubts of the assembly. Ānanda’s body resembled that of the Buddha, being only three finger-widths shorter; the assembly had doubted whether it was the World-Honored One Śākyamuni appearing again, or a Buddha from another direction who had come, or perhaps Ānanda himself had attained Buddhahood.
Once he chanted "Thus have I heard," these three doubts were immediately dispelled.
This is an explanation by way of counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*).

Ānanda, as a disciple, follows worldly convention in saying "I heard"; yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is neither self nor hearing. All ancient commentators have reached this same single conclusion regarding these causal conditions.
Regarding the explanation according to the provisional teachings, the *Śāstra* states:
"Ordinary beings have three kinds of self: those of view, pride, and name; those in training have two kinds; and those beyond training have one kind."

"Ānanda is a seeker who is free from the false notion of self and is able to subdue pride; he uses the conventional designation 'self' according to worldly custom without fault. This explains "self" according to the intention of the Tripiṭaka.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
"To claim 'I' in any of the four propositions is to fall into false views; within the Buddha’s True Dharma there is no self—who, then, would hear it?
This employs the perspective of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Ānanda, the man of much learning, knows that 'self' and 'non-self' are non-dual, yet he discriminates between self and non-self as a pair.
This employs the intent of the Separate Teaching (*prthaktva-naya*).

Furthermore, Ānanda knows that "self" and "non-self" are non-dual; yet he serves as an attendant through skillful means to transmit and uphold the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom. Using his sovereign voice to transmit both the provisional and the ultimate—what could be improper in this?
This uses the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) to explain "I.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* clarifies three Ānandas:
Ānanda (translated as "Joy" [Huānxǐ]), who upholds the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
Ānandabhadra, translated here as "Joyous Sage," received and upheld the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*;
Ānandasāgara, translated here as "Joyous Ocean," upheld the *Buddha-piṭaka*.
In the *Āgama-sūtras*, there is also an Ānanda of the *Mahānidāna-piṭaka* who upheld the *Bodhisattva-piṭaka*.
This refers to a single person who possesses the four virtues and transmits the four Dharma-gates; thus, the meaning is self-evident, and so forth.

Regarding the interpretation in terms of the provisional (迹) and the fundamental (本): if one has not yet realized their convergence, one may say that Ānanda is called "I" in accordance with worldly convention;

however, if one reveals the provisional to manifest the fundamental—having simultaneously resolved his mind for enlightenment under the Buddha King of Emptiness (空王佛)—then what could he not accomplish by skillfully manifesting himself as the transmitter of the Dharma?

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: one contemplates that phenomena produced by causes and conditions are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way. "Simultaneously empty" means that there is no self and no non-self; "simultaneously provisionally existent" means the discriminated self; "simultaneously the Middle Way" means the true, wondrous self, and so forth.

Regarding the explanation of "hearing": Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained the Way and attended upon him for more than twenty years; prior to attending the Buddha, he presumably had not heard [the teachings].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When Ānanda was compiling the Dharma, he said of himself:
'When the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma, I did not see it at that time; thus I heard it through successive transmission.'"
One should know that he did not hear everything.
The ancient commentary states:
"Ānanda attained the Buddha-awakening samādhi, by the power of which he was able to hear it himself."
The *Sūtra on Requiting Kindness* states:
"Ānanda requested four vows, among which he vowed that any sūtras he had not yet heard would be spoken again by the Buddha.
It further says:
"The Buddha spoke this secretly through his own mouth. The *Garbha-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha extended a golden arm from his golden coffin and once again manifested for Ānanda the signs of entering the womb—things heard in all the sūtras."
How much more so when it is spoken of in other places?
This text states:
"When Ānanda received his prediction, he immediately recalled his original vow; the teachings of the former Buddhas that he upheld were all as they are now."
This is the explanation according to the causal conditions (*nidāna*).

As for the explanation according to the teaching (*dharmaparyāya*): Ānanda was filled with joy; his face was like the pure full moon, and his eyes were like blue lotuses. He personally received the Buddha’s instructions as one holds up a perfect vessel, and he transmitted them to transform others as one pours from one vessel into another—this is "hearing by transmission" (*anussava*) and "hearing the Dharma" (*dhammassavana*).

The Joyful Sage, dwelling on the stage of training, attains emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; his faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue are without leakage, and he upholds the teachings he has heard as well as those he has not yet heard.
The Elder Ānanda has received and retained a vast treasury of teachings, like a great cloud holding rain; this is the transmission and upholding of the "dharma that was not heard.

Ānanda is an ocean of learning, a man of great erudition who naturally understands both the permanent and the impermanent. If one knows that the Tathāgata is eternally non-preaching, this is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with great learning. The waters of the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma flow into the heart of Ānanda; this is the transmission and upholding of the "dharma that was not heard."
Now, Ānanda, this sutra is that which you uphold—the wondrous Dharma of "not hearing what is not heard.

Regarding the explanation of the provisional and the fundamental (honji-suijaku): as with the four types of "hearing" mentioned above, they are all provisional manifestations; however, the fundamental ground is inconceivable, and so forth.

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: contemplating the dharma of causes and conditions is the contemplation of hearing what is heard; contemplating emptiness is the contemplation of hearing what is not heard; contemplating the provisional is the contemplation of not hearing what is heard; and contemplating the Middle is the contemplation of neither hearing nor not hearing, and so forth.
"One moment of contemplation" refers to wondrous contemplation, and so forth.
Regarding "at one time," Master Zhao said:
"The time when the Dharma King initiates his auspicious enterprise" refers to the world.
The Treatise says:
"Kāla is real time," which indicates the time for the inner disciples;
as for putting on one's robes at the time of eating, this is for the sake of human beings.
The statement, “*Samaya* is a provisional time,” serves as an antidote for those who hold the false views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
If time were to coincide with the Path, it would be the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and so forth.
If one refers to those above the stage of seeing the truths (darśana-mārga) and below the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), it is called the lower simultaneous [attainment];
if three persons enter the primary truth (paramārtha) together, it is called the middle simultaneous [attainment];
and if they have ascended to the stages (bhūmi) and above, it is called the upper simultaneous [attainment].
If one has already attained the first stage and above, it is called the "superlative single occasion.
This sutra belongs to the superlative single occasion; this is the analysis according to the teaching (*yāna*).
Regarding the fundamental and the trace: the various single occasions mentioned previously are the trace.
The "one time" (ekakṣaṇa) that has been truly attained for a long duration is the fundamental basis.

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*): one contemplates the mind as first empty, then provisional, and finally the Middle Way; this is the sequential contemplation of the mind.
To contemplate the mind as being simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way is the perfect and subtle contemplation of the mind.
As for "Buddha," at the beginning of an eon there is no illness, while at the end of an eon there is much illness;
during times of long life there is happiness, and during times of short life there is suffering.

In the eastern regions of the world, people are wealthy and long-lived; in the western regions, there are many jewels, pearls, oxen, and sheep; in the northern regions, there is no sense of self and no subjects. In such times and places, one does not encounter the appearance of a Buddha.

During the time when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years and during the time it was one hundred years, in Jambudvīpa people practiced the causes before seeing the fruits; therefore, the Buddha appeared in that land.
A Licchavi said:
"The kingdom of Magadha is like a great pond, and the appearance of the Buddha in that country is like a great lotus flower."

Ajita said: "The Buddha is impartial toward all sentient beings and without partiality; it is you who are addicted to the five desires and fail to see the Buddha, not that the Buddha has abandoned you and departed from Magadha."
These are all explanations based on worldly analogies.
If the sun were not to rise, the lotuses in the pond—both those not yet born and those already grown—would undoubtedly wither and die;

if a Buddha appears in the world, there will be kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, the four heavenly kings, and so forth, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). These are explanations based on the human condition.

The faculties and dispositions of those belonging to the three vehicles can induce the appearance of a Buddha in the world, whereas others cannot; they thoroughly sever the seeds of the Peak of Existence and forever cross the stream of birth and death—this is explained from the perspective of the antidote.

The Buddha is neither moved nor emerges from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), yet he enables sentient beings to perceive movement and emergence; in truth, however, there is no movement or emergence in the Tathāgata—this is spoken according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
All of this is merely an explanation based on causes and conditions.

The Buddha is called the Awakened One and the Knower; beneath the tree of the site of enlightenment, he awakened to and knew both the mundane and supramundane general and specific characteristics. His awakening to the mundane consists of suffering and its origin, while his awakening to the supramundane consists of the path and cessation;
furthermore, he is able to awaken others.
Standing six feet tall and eighty years of age, he has the appearance of an elderly bhikṣu.

One who, beneath the Bodhi tree, has exhausted both the outflows (*āsrava*) and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) through thirty-four moments of mind, is a Tripiṭaka Buddha who has awakened himself and awakened others.

Manifesting the body of a distinguished Buddha while wearing the robes of a bhikṣu, one attains a single thought-moment of resonance beneath a tree; for one who has severed all remaining residual habits, this is the penetration of the Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.
To manifest only the extraordinary marks (*vyañjana-lakṣaṇa*), sitting upon a lotus pedestal to receive the office of a Buddha, refers to the distinct Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.
To conceal the previous three marks and manifest only the inconceivable mark like empty space refers to the perfect Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"Some see the Tathāgata’s body as sixteen feet tall; some see it as a small body or a large body; some see him seated upon a flower pedestal, expounding the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for hundreds of thousands of Śākyamunis; or they see his body identical to empty space, pervading the entire Dharmadhātu without any discrimination."
This is precisely that meaning.
This constitutes the analysis according to the teachings (*yàojiào fēnbié*).

Regarding the explanation in terms of the fundamental and the manifested (*běnjì shì*): one Buddha is the fundamental, while the three Buddhas are the manifested. The repeated manifestations of birth and the repeated proclamations of extinction occurring in the interim are all manifestations.

Regarding the statement that "only the four Buddhas of the *Mūla-bhūmi* are fundamental," the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*) is as follows: to contemplate the mind produced by causes and conditions as first empty, then provisional, and finally the Middle Way constitutes partial enlightenment;
to contemplate the mind as simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle is perfect enlightenment, and so forth.

Regarding "abiding" (sthiti): it is that which can abide and that which is abided in. That which is abided in is the royal city of the Sahā world; that which can abide consists of the four modes of deportment. To abide in the world without perishing—this is the explanation of "abiding" in terms of the causes and conditions of the world.
Furthermore, "abiding" refers to abiding in the ten paths of wholesome action and abiding within the four dhyānas; this is the explanation of "abiding" in terms of human causes and conditions.
Furthermore, "abiding" refers to abiding in the three samādhis; this is the explanation of "abiding" in terms of remedial causes and conditions.
Furthermore, regarding "abiding": to abide in Śūraṅgama is precisely to explain abiding through the causes and conditions of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and so forth.

Regarding the classification by teaching (*yàojiào*): the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka, through the gate of analytical reduction (*pīkṣā-mukha*), gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*) and abides in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
The Universal Buddha (Samantabhadra) issues forth from the gate of essence to realize the truth, abiding in both *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇa.
The Particular Buddha (Pratyekabuddha) enters through the gate of sequential stages, abiding in the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*).
The Perfect Buddha enters through the gate of non-succession and abides in the Secret Treasury.
The abidings of the three preceding Buddhas involve both subject and object as being coarse;
the abiding of the final Buddha involves both subject and object as being subtle.
The present sutra is precisely the Perfect Buddha abiding in the wondrous abode.

Regarding the explanation of the fundamental and the manifested: while the Buddha of the Tripitaka should enter nirvana, out of compassion he manifests traces, taking birth in a physical body that dwells in the world.
The Buddhas of the Shared [Vehicle] rely on their vows and compassion to assist residual habits in performing Buddha-work for the sake of delivering sentient beings.

As for the Distinctive and Perfect [Vehicles], both Buddhas permeate the *dharmatā* with compassion; out of pity for sentient beings, they manifest responsive transformations throughout the *dharmadhātu*.

It should be known that the four Buddhas abide in the abode of the fundamental Buddha; out of compassion, they abide in the royal city of the Endurance Land (Sahā), remaining in the world through their majestic deportment—this is called "abiding as a trace."

Regarding "contemplative understanding" (kuan-jie): contemplation abides in an object—whether it be the object of impermanence, or the objects that are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way. Because it abides in these objects by means of the dharma of non-abiding, it is called "abiding."

Regarding "Rājagṛha" (the City of Royal Residence): in India it is called Rājagṛha; "Rāja" here means "king" and "gṛha" here means "city. The name of the country is Magadha, which here means "Non-Harming," as there was no law of execution there.
It is also called Māgadha, which here means "Heavenly Net"; "Heavenly Net" is the name of a king, and the country was named after that king—this king being the father of Śarabha.

In the distant past, during a long-elapsed kalpa, this king ruled over a thousand small kingdoms. While the king was touring the mountains, he encountered a female lion; the multitude fled in all directions, yet she coupled with the king.

When the subsequent month was full, he was born upon the palace roof. The king, knowing him to be his own son, proclaimed, "I have no children; this one has been granted by Heaven. He was raised as the crown prince. Because there were mottled spots on his feet, the people of the time called him Pāṇḍu-pāda (the Mottled-foot).

Later, upon succeeding to the throne, he took pleasure in eating meat and commanded his cooks never to let the supply run short. When one day there was suddenly a shortage, he took a small child who had recently died west of the city to serve as his meal.

The king said, "This is most excellent," and commanded that this meat be prepared regularly. The kitchen attendants daily captured one person, causing the entire kingdom to be filled with grief and fear. The kings of a thousand small nations raised armies and deposed him, placing him in Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. There, the rākṣasas assisted him as a king of ghosts; he then made a vow with the mountain deity, swearing to take a thousand kings to sacrifice to the mountain.
He captured nine hundred and ninety-nine, missing only King Puming; later, he watched for an opportunity and seized him.
The king wept bitterly, lamenting that his lifelong practice of truthful speech had now been betrayed by his own word.

Bōzú released him and he returned to his kingdom, where he established great acts of charity and installed his crown prince; yet he proceeded to his death with a joyful countenance and a peaceful mind.
When Bōzú questioned him about this, he replied:
"I was able to hear the Holy Dharma."
He then commanded him to preach, extensively praising the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and censuring killing; he further recited the four verses on impermanence (*anitya*), and so forth.
Upon hearing the Dharma, Baka attained the stage of the equality of emptiness, which is the first bhūmi.
The thousand kings each took a drop of blood and three strands of hair to offer as a vow to the mountain deity.

Vṛṣabha established Śrāvastī together with the thousand kings; they made the Five Mountains their capital as a great kingdom, each entrusting a thousand small kingdoms to his descendants, while the thousand kings took turns governing the affairs of the great kingdom.
Furthermore, while the common people were living within the Five Mountains, they built their dwellings seven times and were burned out seven times. The people deliberated, saying:

"It is because of our meager merit that we are repeatedly reduced to ashes; yet the King, by virtue of his power of merit, has his dwellings unburned. From this day forward, we shall all vacate our houses to serve as the King's residence."
Because they were spared from being burned by this means, it is called Rājagṛha (the King’s House).
Furthermore, because a thousand kings, including Aśvajit, established their residence on that site, it is called Rājagṛha.

Moreover, when Aśvajit attained the Way, he granted amnesty to the thousand kings; since those thousand kings were pardoned on that ground, the place was named Rāja-śeṣa (the King’s Amnesty), and the sūtra author merely borrowed the phonetics for the word "house" (gṛha).
The causes and conditions for this are set forth in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and various sutras, and so forth.
Regarding the teaching (*yàojiào*), the *Sutra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma* states:

"The visions of the entire great assembly differ: some see the Śāla grove as being entirely composed of earth, sand, grass, trees, and stone walls; some see it as pure and adorned with the seven treasures; some see this grove as the place where the Buddhas of the three periods of time travel; and some see this grove as the true dharma-body of the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas."
By understanding this principle through examples, one sees that while the four views differ, just as that which is dwelt upon is so, that which dwells therein is likewise so.

This is an analysis according to the teachings (*śāsana*). The aspects of the fundamental and the manifested (*mūla-vyākṛta*), as well as the contemplation of the mind (*citta-bhāvanā*), will be discussed later.
"Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata" is translated here as "Spiritual Vulture Peak," also called "Vulture Head," and also "Wolf’s Footprint. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty stated:
"It is the 'Wangju' mentioned by the poets in the *Guanzhui* [of the *Classic of Poetry*]."
The *Erya* states: "It resembles an owl (*chi*).
Furthermore, it is explained that the mountain peaks resemble vultures (*jiao*), and thus the peaks are named after the bird.

It is further said that to the south of the mountain there is a Śītavana forest; because vultures eat corpses there and then perch upon the mountain, people of the time called it Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa).

Another interpretation holds that former Buddhas and present Buddhas all resided on this mountain: after a Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Arhats dwell there; when the Dharma has ceased, Pratyekabuddhas dwell there; and where there are no Pratyekabuddhas, spirits and deities dwell there.
Since this is the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, it possesses three characteristics in total, for which reason it is called Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa).
There are five viharas:
Vaibhāra-vatsa, which is translated here as "Cave of the Lord of Heaven" (Indrakīla); [and others].
Saptaparṇa-guha, here translated as "Cave of the Seven Leaves";
Indrākṣa-guha, here translated as "Snake Mountain";
Śabdavatsa-ṛkṣaka-parvata, here translated as "Mountain of the Young Solitary Power."
The fifth is Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
Question:
When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and heaven and earth are cleared away, how can Buddhas of the past and Buddhas of the future cohabit on this mountain?
Answer: When the subsequent kalpa is established, the original characteristics reappear; those who have attained supernatural powers (ṛddhi) know the ancient names and apply them to the present.
This is, for example, like how in a previous kalpa there was a clan named Gautama, and one uses that original clan name to designate the present.
Regarding the explanation of "mountain" according to the provisional teachings (*yōkyō*), it is as stated in the analogy of the city, and so forth.

Regarding the explanation through contemplation (*kanshaku*): the "king" is the mind-king (*cittarāja*), and the "house" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The mind-king constructs this house; if one analyzes the house of the five aggregates until it is empty, that emptiness constitutes the city of *nirvāṇa*. This contemplation is shallow, like merely seeing the earth and wood.
If one realizes that the house of the five aggregates is itself empty, and that emptiness is the city of *nirvāṇa*, this is the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

If one contemplates the house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and, through the cessation of this form (*rūpa*), attains eternal form—wherein feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise so—these four virtues are the dwelling place of all Buddhas.

If one contemplates the five aggregates as the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and since the dharma-nature is devoid of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, all sentient beings are themselves nirvāṇa; they cannot be further extinguished, for they are ultimately empty and quiescent. This house of ultimate emptiness and stillness—such nirvāṇa—is the true reality of *tathatā*, and so forth.

Regarding the contemplation of the Mountain of the Mind: if one contemplates the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it is like a mountain of insentience; the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is like the spirit; and the three [other] aggregates are like the vultures. To contemplate this Spirit-Vulture as impermanent is the analytical contemplation (*vibhāga-vipaśyanā*);
to contemplate this Spirit-Vulture as emptiness is the contemplation of essence (*tattva-vipaśyanā*).

Contemplating the Spirit as the nature of wisdom—the factor of penetration—is the adornment of wisdom; the Vultures as the accumulated conditions—the factor of origination—are the adornment of merit; and the Mountain as the true cause of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is the immovable triad of dharmas, called the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*).
Abiding therein oneself and also using it to deliver others, as the subsequent text states:
"The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna," which refers to the two contemplations of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], and so forth.

"Middle" means that the Buddha favored the Middle Way: his ascent to heaven was at midday, his descent was in the central land, and his parinirvāṇa occurred at midnight—all of these symbolize the Middle Way;
now, dwelling in the mountains, he teaches the Middle Way.
The explanation of the assembly of fellow listeners is threefold:
first, the śrāvakas; second, the bodhisattvas; and third, the miscellaneous assembly. Most sūtras follow this pattern.
The older tradition states that these categories correspond to "having the facts" (有事) and "having the meaning" (有義).

Regarding the "matters" [of their physical forms and traces]: the Śrāvakas pursue forms and traces that are close to the Tathāgata; as they have left the mundane net and their traces are near those of the Tathāgata, their realization of the sūtras constitutes their closeness, and thus they are listed first.
The devas and humans differ in form and attire, and their traces do not consist of service and attendance; as their realization of the sūtras constitutes their distance, they are listed last.

The Bodhisattvas do not regulate their physical forms and have no fixed traces; since they are neither like the laity nor like the monastic community, they occupy a position between the "junior" and the "senior," and are therefore placed in the middle.

Regarding the meaning of "being between": Śrāvakas delight in nirvāṇa, while devas and humans are attached to saṃsāra; each has a partiality. The Bodhisattva neither delights nor is attached, but dwells in the middle seeking the fundamental principle; therefore, he stands between the two.

The intent of the *Śāstra* is likewise. This single interpretation appears as two: the "explanation of the matter" resembles the *nidāna* (causal conditions), while the "explanation of the meaning" resembles the *yathāśāsana* (according to the teachings), and so forth.

Regarding the explanation of the "Original and Traces": how could a śrāvaka, who secretly maintains [the bodhisattva vow] within while manifesting externally, ever have been fixed in the realization of nirvāṇa?
And since both devas and humans are all great *sattvas*, how could they possibly remain immersed in the defilements of saṃsāra?
All of these are traces that lead away from the two extremes, while the fundamental reality is always the Middle Way.
Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional breaks through [attachment to] birth-and-death exclusively;

the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness breaks through [clinging to] nirvana exclusively; and the correct contemplation of the Middle Way has no such sequence of before and after, and so forth.
The śrāvakas are divided into two groups:
first the bhikṣus, followed by the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣus are further divided into two:
First, those with extensive knowledge are listed, followed by those with limited knowledge;
these were formerly referred to as "those of great renown" and "those of minor renown.
Although this lacks textual authority, I have now judged it according to the text in this manner.
Regarding the six aspects of the assembly of those with great knowledge:
first, their category; second, their number; third, their status; fourth, their praise; fifth, the listing of names;
and sixth, the conclusion. First, as for the category: they all belong to the class of great bhikṣus.
For example, among the various regions and classes of people, each has its own rank and status.
Now, these bhikṣus are all well-known to the multitude, highly esteemed, and of great virtue.

The *Śāstra* clarifies that "together" (*yǔ*) carries the meaning of "in common. Taking the seven items as an illustration to explain this commonality, they are: one time, one place, one precept, one mind, one view, one path, and one liberation.
If categorized according to the teachings, each should clarify seven sets of seven:

one set of seven for each of the Three Baskets (Tripitaka), two sets of seven for the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), immeasurable sets of seven for the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), and one set of seven for the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

If one has not yet revealed their true identity, this refers precisely to the sevenfold structure within the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, which directly clarifies the similarities and differences between two perspectives: while time, place, precepts, and liberation are the same, the three aspects of mind, view, and path differ;
once one reaches the stage where the Three are opened to reveal the One, one then enters the sevenfold structure of the Perfect Teaching.
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Lotus Sūtra Commentary) explains four types of śrāvakas; here, those who abide in the fruit are further divided into two:

those who abide in the fruit by analyzing phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) are the śrāvakas of the Tripiṭaka teaching, while those who abide in the fruit by realizing the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are the śrāvakas of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*).
The opening of the responsive manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) is twofold:

the responsive manifestation for those who have ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*), which refers to the *śrāvakas* of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*); and the responsive manifestation for those who have ascended to the abodes (*vihāra*), which refers to the *śrāvakas* of the Perfect Teaching (*samyaksambuddhayāna*).
The opening of the Buddha-way for *śrāvakas* is likewise twofold:

Causing others to hear the Buddha-way through a gradual sequence constitutes the *pratyekabuddha-śrāvaka* (separate teaching śrāvaka); causing others to hear the Buddha-way without a sequential order constitutes the *pariniṣpanna-śrāvaka* (perfect śrāvaka).
The meaning of "śrāvaka" is vast and profound; how then can it be defined solely by those who have realized *nirvāṇa*, and so forth?

Regarding the term "Great" (*mahā*): the *Śāstra* explains that "Great" signifies both "many" and "superior. It is called "Great" because its capacity and measure are revered by great beings such as celestial kings; it is called "superior" because it transcends the ninety-five types of heterodox paths; it is called "many" because it possesses comprehensive knowledge of both internal and external scriptures, and furthermore, because its numerical count reaches twelve thousand.
Now, it is called "Great" because there is a Great Way, a Great Function, and Great Knowledge; therefore, it is said to be "Great.
It is called "Victorious" because the Way is victorious, the Function is victorious, and Knowledge is victorious; therefore, it is said to be "Victorious."
"Much" refers to the abundance of the Path, the abundance of its application, and the abundance of its knowledge; hence it is called "much.
The Path is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), which is superior to all non-Buddhist paths of omniscience;
its application is the shared foundation of mindfulness (*sāmānyasmṛtyupasthāna*), which excels the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of non-Buddhists.
"Knowledge" refers to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); it primarily refers to the four Vedas and the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

Regarding the explanation of "Great," "Many," and "Victorious" according to the teachings (*yathāśāsana*), such as "honored by great beings" and so forth, these are merely explanations within the Tripitaka.
"Great" means being revered by Arhats of great power;
"many" means thoroughly knowing that arising and ceasing are themselves the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing;
and "supreme" means surpassing the three baskets and four gates—this is the explanation according to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
Furthermore, "Great" means that his person is one whom the Arhats of great power revere;
"Many" means that he knows all the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and "Victorious" means that he surpasses those of the Two Vehicles—this is the explanation according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
Furthermore, "Great" means that which is revered by all the great Bodhisattvas;
"Many" means that one fully knows the immeasurable dharmas of the Dharma-realm;
and "Victorious" means surpassing all other Bodhisattvas—this is the explanation according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Regarding the "Original and the Traces": these great virtuous ones have long been praised by all Buddhas; they originally attained the *Vaijayanta-samādhi* (Victorious Banner Samādhi) and transcended all non-Buddhists. Having already accomplished the omniscience of the *sarvajñatā*, they manifest as traces to assist the Buddha in his transformative work. They appear as the greatest, most numerous, and most excellent among those with craving and views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi*), desiring to lead the "milk" into "curd.
Furthermore, they appear as the greatest, most numerous, and most excellent among the Tripitaka, desiring to lead the "curd" into "fresh butter.
They appear as the greatest, most numerous, and most excellent within the Vaipulya sutras, desiring to lead the "fresh butter" into "ripened butter."
It is said that by manifesting the turning of the teaching, he produced the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, and the *Śatasāhasrikā* as the Great, the Many, and the Supreme;

and because he wished to draw the matured cream into the clarified butter (*sarpis*), he produced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the Great, the Many, and the Supreme—yet its original ground is once again the Great, the Many, and the Supreme, and so forth.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the contemplation of emptiness is "great," the contemplation of the provisional is "many," and the contemplation of the middle is "supreme.
Furthermore, because the nature of the mind within the direct contemplation of the middle is vast and expansive like empty space, it is called "great";
because it simultaneously negates both extremes and enters the ocean of quiescent extinction, it is called "supreme."
The dual illumination of the two truths contains much within it; because one mind encompasses all minds, it is called "much.
Regarding the term "bhikṣu," Master Zao said:

"In the Qin language, it means 'pure livelihood. It carries four meanings—begging for food, destroying afflictions, being able to uphold the precepts, and terrifying Māra—in the Indic language. Since there was no corresponding term in the Qin language to translate these, the original appellation was retained."
Master Kumārajīva said:
"When first leaving the home of wife and children, one should support oneself by begging for alms, living a pure life;
when finally leaving the home of the triple world, one must destroy the afflictions and maintain the precepts to guard oneself."
"Possessing these two meanings, the celestial Māras fear that he will transcend their realm. The *Śāstra* states:

"Frightening Māra, destroying evil, and mendicant—Māra delights in birth and death; since he has already left the household life and further transforms others, causing them all to depart from the triple world and oppose Māra’s intent, Māra attempts to restrain him by force but instead finds himself bound with the five fetters. He can do nothing but grieve and fear; therefore, he is called 'one who frightens Māra.'"
Those who have left the household life must destroy the seven evils of body and speech;

therefore, they are said to "destroy evil. Now, for those living at home, there are three lawful means of livelihood: first, agriculture; second, commerce; and third, service, used to sustain one's physical life.

For those who have left the household life, the Buddha did not permit these; rather, they rely solely on alms to sustain themselves. When their bodies are at peace, the Way endures, and they bring benefit and merit to their donors—these three principles mutually supporting one another constitute the meaning of a *bhikṣu*.
In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*, the mention of the bhikṣu named Bhinnakarma is incomplete.

Here, by clarifying these three meanings, one should understand them as applying to both the beginning and the end. For example, at the time of initial ordination, through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the power of the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) pervades all objects, thereby overturning unmanifest evil.

At the initial cultivation of dhyāna and samādhi, the precept co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*) is produced, which restrains and subdues the greed and anger of the mental ground so that they do not arise.
When one first cultivates contemplative wisdom, the "similar path" (anuloma-mārga) arises together with the precepts, which are capable of subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why is it that only the final moment of mind is called the "destruction of evil," while the initial moment is not?

As for "terrifying Māra": when one first shaves the hair and receives the precepts, one already causes Māra to grieve; when cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to subdue the afflictions and cultivating wisdom (*prajñā*) to destroy the afflictions, the initial moment of mind likewise causes Māra to fear—why then is it said that only the final moment does so?

Regarding the "mendicant" (bhikṣu): one who initially abandons wrong livelihood and sustains themselves by begging; one who practices meditation through various objects; one who seeks concentration and cultivates wisdom by taking principles as their object to seek the outflow-free (anāsrava); all such individuals are mendicants—how much more so those who are in actual correspondence with the path? How could they not be mendicants?
Because they possess these meanings, they are collectively termed *bhikṣus*.
However, according to the Sūtra masters, this refers specifically to the *bhikṣu* of the final mind; such is the intent of the Tripiṭaka.

If one seeks the true name of a "beggar" (*bhikṣu*) by traversing conditions, and if one is called a "destroyer of evil" for destroying the delusions regarding principles that obstruct [enlightenment], and practices this way while fearing the four Māras, then this accords with the general meaning of the Teaching.

If one seeks the principle by traversing the three truths, they are called a "beggar" (bhikṣu); if they eliminate both the pervasive and specific delusions, they are called "one who destroys evil. As for "fearing the eight māras and ten māras," this refers specifically to the distinct [delusions].

If one seeks the flavor of the true mark within birth and death itself, they are called a "beggar" (bhikṣu); if one realizes that afflictions are themselves bodhi, they are called "one who destroys evil. That the realm of Māra is itself the realm of the Buddha is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

If one has not yet revealed their original station (*honji*), only the former two meanings are clarified; if one has already manifested their fundamental nature, the latter intention is fully realized.

Regarding the fundamental and the phenomenal (*honjaku*): fundamentally, one ascends to the summit of the Mountain of Nirvana and parts from the parents of ignorance, delusion, and craving, as well as the wife and children of karmic fetters and afflictions; having emerged from the households of the *pariccheda-vipariṇāma-śīla* (limited) and *pariṇāmi-śīla* (transformative) births, and having long since eliminated the five stages of dwelling, what evil is there that is not destroyed?
Having attained the true joy of the Dharma, one is like one who has eaten milk-gruel and requires nothing more.
By upholding the Middle Way and the precepts of the Śīlapāramitā that accompany it, one subdues the realm of Māra; this is the suchness of the Buddha-realm.

Capable of being ridden and controlled, having long since accomplished the merits of his original ground, he manifests traces of the five flavors of the Dharma to harmonize sentient beings and leads them forward as a bhikṣu, as explained previously.

As for "contemplating the mind," it means contemplating that a single thought-moment is as pure as empty space, unimpeded by the shackles of the two extremes; when great wisdom is equanimous, non-abiding, and non-attached, this is called "leaving home.
Sustaining the life-force of the Dharma-body through the wisdom of the Middle Way is called "begging for sustenance" (bhikṣu).
Contemplating that the afflictions of the five stages are themselves bodhi is called "destroying evil."
All extremes and inversions are none other than the Middle Way; this is what is meant by "frightening the Māras," and so forth. Regarding the term "assembly" (*saṃgha*):

in India it is called *saṃgha*, which here translates as "harmonious assembly. A single person does not constitute a harmonious assembly; only from four people upward is it termed a harmonious assembly. In terms of affairs, there is harmony because there is no separate group; in terms of Dharma, there is harmony because there is no separate principle.

The Buddha was constantly accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people: the three Kāśyapas with their one thousand followers, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana with two hundred and fifty, and it is further said that Yaśas had fifty.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 45, states:

"Among the five hundred bhikṣus, ninety possessed the three types of clear knowledge (*traividya*), ninety were liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), and the remainder were liberated through wisdom alone (*prajñā-vimukta*)."
The *Śāstra* elucidates four kinds of Saṃgha:

those who do not rely on pure precepts are called the "precept-breaking Saṃgha"; those who do not understand the laws and regulations are called the "deluded Saṃgha"; those at the stage of the five expedient means are called the "ashamed Saṃgha"; and those from the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) onward are called the "true Saṃgha."
Among these, it is not the three types [of Saṃgha], but rather the true Saṃgha.

If one relies on the four teachings, this Saṃgha has passed through the five flavors of the partial and the perfect, acting as a fellow listener; now, this is precisely the testimony of faith within the Perfect Teaching.

Regarding the interpretation through the perspectives of the fundamental and the trace: the fundamental [truth] is in harmony with the principle of the true aspect (*bhūtatathatā*), and it is also in harmony with the karmic conditions of sentient beings within the dharma-realm; meanwhile, the trace manifests as the Sangha of both provisional and ultimate phenomena and principles, guiding all sentient beings throughout the five flavors, and so forth.

Regarding those who practice through contemplative understanding: when a beginner enters the stage of "semblance contemplation" (*sādharmya-darśana*) within the Middle Way but has not yet realized the truth, they feel shame before the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*) and remorse before the various sages; such are the monks with a sense of shame (*hrīmat*).
